reviews.text: This story understands something profound about how people process guilt differently. Voigt's insomnia, his compulsive memorization of the dead man's details -- bad knees, Sunday phone calls -- these are textbook features of complicated grief, and the story never labels them as such, just lets them sit there for the reader to recognize. But the real psychological portrait is Nora. She reads emotional data with extraordinary precision and then files it in the wrong category every time. She sees Voigt's grief as 'wrong-shaped' and notes it without understanding why. She recognizes the blotter note as pain and categorizes it as leverage. She's not cold; she's a specific kind of intelligent person who has built a system for understanding human behavior that works perfectly until it encounters something her system wasn't designed to hold. The last scene -- the French press from her mother, the call she doesn't make -- devastated me. She doesn't know she's lonely. She has filed it under 'personality.'
